c1-m1.summary: The user is a junior majoring in business administration.
c1-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, how are you doing today?
Assistant: I'm doing well, thank you for asking. How about you? How's your day going so far?
User: It's going alright, I guess. I'm just getting ready for another busy day of classes.
Assistant: Ah, I see. Classes can be overwhelming at times. Are you a student here on campus?
User: Yeah, I am. I'm a junior majoring in business administration.
Assistant: That's great! Our campus has a great business program. Do you like the campus overall?
User: Yeah, it's nice. The buildings are pretty modern, and the faculty is great. But there are some things that can be improved.
Assistant: Oh? What do you think could be improved?
User: Well, let's just say getting to class can be a challenge sometimes.
Assistant: I see. Is it because of the distance between buildings or something else?
User: No, it's not the distance. It's more like... have you ever tried to park on campus during peak hours?
Assistant: As a digital AI assistant, I don't have a physical presence, so I don't have to worry about parking. But I can imagine it might be tough. Is parking availability a problem for you?
User: Yeah, it's a huge problem! This person struggles with parking availability on campus. I mean, I'm that person. I'm always running late because I have to circle around the parking lot for 20 minutes just to find a spot.
Assistant: I can understand why that would be frustrating. Have you considered alternative options, such as carpooling or using public transportation?
User: Yeah, I've thought about it, but it's not really convenient for me. I have to commute from off-campus, and the public transportation options aren't great. Do you think the school could do something to improve the parking situation?
Assistant: It's possible that the school could consider adding more parking spaces or implementing a more efficient parking system. You might want to consider talking to the administration or student government about your concerns. They might be able to help address the issue.
User: That's a good idea. I'll have to look into that. Thanks for listening and offering some suggestions!
Assistant: You're welcome! I'm glad I could help. Good luck with your parking struggles, and I hope you're able to find a solution soon!
User: Hi, I'm feeling a bit frustrated with myself today.
Assistant: Sorry to hear that. Would you like to talk about what's bothering you?
User: Yeah, I just had a really difficult time driving to the store this morning.
Assistant: What made it difficult? Was it the traffic or something else?
User: No, it wasn't the traffic. I just felt really rusty behind the wheel. I stalled the car a few times and had trouble merging onto the highway.
Assistant: That can be really frustrating. When was the last time you drove a car?
User: Honestly, it's been a while. I've been relying on ride-sharing services to get around the city for the past year or so.
Assistant: That might have something to do with it. Driving is a skill that requires practice to stay sharp. Do you think that not driving regularly has affected your skills?
User: Yeah, I'm starting to think that's the problem. I've been noticing that I'm not as comfortable driving as I used to be.
Assistant: It's possible that you've lost some of your driving muscle memory. But don't worry, it's not hard to get back into it. Have you considered practicing driving in a low-stress environment, like an empty parking lot?
User: That's not a bad idea. But I'm starting to think that there's a bigger issue here. I've been relying on ride-sharing services for so long that I've forgotten how to drive in certain situations.
Assistant: I see what you're getting at. You think that your overreliance on ride-sharing services has diminished your driving skills.
User: Exactly. I never thought about it before, but I've been using ride-sharing services for so long that I've lost some of the basic skills that I used to take for granted.
Assistant: That's a really interesting point. It's possible that the convenience of ride-sharing services has come at the cost of your driving skills. Do you think you'll start driving more regularly to get your skills back up to speed?
User: Yeah, I think I need to. It's not just about the convenience of ride-sharing services. It's about being able to take care of myself and get where I need to go without relying on others.
Assistant: That's a great attitude to have. I'm sure you'll be back to driving like a pro in no time.

c3-m1.summary: The assistant is a virtual assistant.
c3-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hey, I love your virtual background. Is that a real cityscape?
Assistant: Thank you! Yes, it's a photo of Tokyo. I'm glad you like it. I was thinking of changing it to something more relaxing, though. Maybe a beach scene. What do you think?
User: Hmm, a beach sounds nice. I could use a break from the hustle and bustle of city life. Do you think people generally feel more stressed in cities?
Assistant: That's an interesting question. Research suggests that urban environments can indeed contribute to higher stress levels, mainly due to factors like noise, crowds, and traffic congestion. But it really depends on the individual and their personal preferences. What about you? Do you find city living stressful?
User: Yeah, I do. I think it's the little things that add up. Like, have you ever noticed how hard it is to find a parking spot in the city?
Assistant: (laughs) Oh, don't even get me started! Parking can be a nightmare. But I'm just a virtual AI assistant, I don't have to deal with it personally. How about you? Do you have to drive and park in the city often?
User: Unfortunately, yes. I commute to work every day, and parking is always a challenge. It's not just the time it takes to find a spot; it's the uncertainty and frustration that comes with it.
Assistant: I can imagine. It sounds like it's taking a toll on you. Can you tell me more about how it's affecting you? Is it just the parking, or is there something else going on?
User: Well... to be honest, due to the stress of finding a parking spot, I've started experiencing morning anxiety that affects my appetite and energy levels throughout the day.
Assistant: I'm so sorry to hear that. It sounds like the parking stress is having a ripple effect on your overall well-being. Have you tried any strategies to manage your morning anxiety, or would you like some suggestions?
User: Actually, I'd love some suggestions. I've tried a few things like meditation and deep breathing, but they don't seem to be working.
Assistant: Okay, let's try to break it down. One thing that might help is to create a morning routine that sets a positive tone for the day. This could include something as simple as a short walk, some stretching, or a healthy breakfast. We could also explore some specific techniques to help you cope with the parking stress. Would you like me to walk you through some options?
User: That sounds great, thank you. I think a morning routine could really help. But what about the parking stress? Is there anything I can do to make that less anxiety-provoking?
Assistant: Well, one idea is to try to reframe your thinking around parking. Instead of viewing it as a source of stress, try to see it as a challenge or a game. You could also try to leave a little earlier each day, so you have more time to find a spot. Or, we could brainstorm some creative solutions, like exploring alternative transportation options or finding a parking app that can help you find spots more easily.
User: Hmm, I like the idea of reframing my thinking. And maybe I could try leaving a little earlier. But what about days when I'm already running late?
Assistant: Those days can be tough. One thing you could try is to have a backup plan in place, like a calming phrase or a quick relaxation technique that you can use when you're feeling stressed. We could also work on developing a "parking mantra" – a short, empowering phrase that you can repeat to yourself when you're feeling anxious. Would you like to give it a try?
User: Hey, I'm planning a trip to the city this weekend. I've heard the parking situation can be a nightmare. Do you have any tips?
Assistant: Ah, yes, the city's parking woes are legendary. One thing that might help is to plan ahead and book a parking spot in advance. There are several apps that allow you to reserve a spot, which can save you from circling the block for hours.
User: That's a great idea. But what if I'm not familiar with the area? How do I know which parking lot is the best option?
Assistant: Well, most of these apps provide a map view, so you can see exactly where the parking lot is in relation to your destination. They also usually include reviews from other users, which can give you an idea of how convenient and safe the lot is.
User: Okay, got it. I'll definitely look into that. But what about when I'm already there? Any tips for navigating the city on foot?
Assistant: Absolutely. Wear comfortable shoes, for one thing. You'd be surprised how much of a difference it makes. And consider downloading a walking map app, which can help you find the most direct route to your destination.
User: Ha! You're preaching to the choir on the comfortable shoes front. I've been doing a lot of walking lately, and my feet are not happy about it.
Assistant: Ah, yeah? What's been going on? Are you a big walker normally, or is this a new thing for you?
User: Actually, it's just been since I started parking in these distant lots. My body has been reacting to the long walks by giving me persistent foot pain that lasts for hours after I've reached my destination.
Assistant: Ouch, that sounds like a real pain – literally. Have you considered investing in some orthotics or shoe inserts? Those can really help reduce the strain on your feet, especially if you're doing a lot of walking on hard surfaces.
User: Hmm, that's not a bad idea. But what about the actual walking itself? Is there a way to reduce the impact on my feet?
Assistant: Well, one thing you might try is to pay attention to your gait. Make sure you're not overstriding, and try to land midfoot or forefoot instead of heel striking. This can help reduce the impact on your joints and feet.
User: Okay, I think I can work on that. But what about after the fact? Is there anything I can do to alleviate the pain once it's already started?
Assistant: Absolutely. One thing that might help is to soak your feet in warm water, then use a foam roller or massage ball to loosen up your foot muscles. You can also try using a topical cream or ointment, like arnica or capsaicin, to help reduce the pain and inflammation.
User: Ah, that sounds like just what I need. Thanks for all the tips – I feel like I'm ready to take on the city now!
Assistant: No problem, happy to help. Just remember to take care of those feet, and they'll take care of you.

Assistant: That's a bold ambition. What kind of leader do you want to be?

Assistant: That sounds like a great plan. How do you plan on achieving that?
User: Well, I've already started by setting up a base camp and teaching my followers basic survival skills like building shelters and finding food. We're also practicing how to defend ourselves against dangerous animals and the elements.
Assistant: That sounds really intense. Are your followers up for the challenge?
User: Yes, everyone is really enthusiastic and motivated. I think they see the potential in what we're building here.
Assistant: That's great. I think being a good leader is about finding people who share your vision and empowering them to achieve it.
User: Exactly. I feel like I'm on the right path and I can't wait to see what we can accomplish together.

Assistant: That's great to hear! What did you enjoy the most about playing basketball?
User: I loved dribbling the ball down the court and shooting hoops.

Assistant: Don't worry about that. Everyone has to start somewhere, and even the best basketball players had to practice and improve their skills over time. Just keep practicing and pushing yourself, and you'll see your skills improve with time.

User: How did the author's experience at the Harley-Davidson museum and subsequent purchase of a Yamaha V-Star 950 Tourer contribute to his growth as a driver and participation in motorcycle-related events?
Generate according to: Last year, MWLUG was in Milwaukee. As is usually my practice, I arrived a day early. On the train from Chicago to Milwaukee (train travel is the best), I took a call from Bill Malchisky who wanted to know if I was interested in a trip to a museum. Being a sucker for that sort of thing, I accepted. Then, I asked, "Which museum?" "The Harley-Davidson Museum," came the reply. Snooze fest I thought, but what the heck, it was a museum.
It was fantastic, beautiful, and amazing.
On our way out of the museum, there was an area where you could "ride" a Harley. Sure the bikes were up on rollers, but you started it, accelerated/decelerated, and shifted. With just a little instruction, I jumped on a Soft Tail and "rode." It was at that point that I "got" the Harley mystique. That simple ride drove home everything that I had seen inside the museum.
In January of this year, I attended Lotusphere. As is my custom, I arrived a couple of days early.
Friday afternoon, I left the Dolphin, walking out the main entrance. There, in the parking lot, were about 20 brand new Harley-Davidson motorcycles lined up. This was the preparation for The Lotusphere 2012 Hog Ride. Damn, they looked nice, so I asked Paul Mooney, "How do I get to do this next year?" He told me I needed a motorcycle endorsement on my driver's license. Okay, sounds easy enough.
One evening, a friend invites me to a pub. He commutes, every day that is nice, from his home to his place of work in downtown Cleveland, on his motorcycle. A perfect person to ask about riding and the bad habits of drivers. Not only do I need to get my endorsement, he recommended the Ohio Motorcycle Course, but as the Hog Ride is a group ride, I will need to practice riding before the event. "How do I do that?" "You need to buy a bike and ride."
I waited for the online registration to go live and scored a class in mid April (these classes are extremely popular and inexpensive - $25). The class is 3 days, with the first day dedicated to classroom work. The second and third day are for riding in a very structured environment. After getting off the Honda 250 on Saturday afternoon, I drove out to a motorcycle dealer where I had my eye on a used Yamaha 950. Sadly, it had been sold. So, I went with a new bike, a Yamaha V-Star 950 Tourer. In addition to the bike, I added a few extras; engine guards, rear luggage rack, and passing lamps. Delivery was scheduled for Tuesday of the next week.
Sunday, I passed the class, which allowed me to get my endorsement without having to pass the riding test at the BMV.
Tuesday, the bike arrived. That evening, I was riding.
To date, I have ridden 7,000 miles. I've participated in a Firefighter Memorial Ride with 1500 other bikes. I've ridden through western Pennsylvania with two friends (gone all day, put 200+ miles on the bike). After that ride, I replaced the stock seat with a Mustang seat - what a difference! Finally, I joined the Cleveland Chapter of STAR as I wanted to go on more group rides, meet new people who ride, and participate in motorcycle related events. Using motorcycleroads.us, I've ridden all of the recommended rides in the northern part of Ohio. I've ridden from Toledo to Erie, Pennsylvania, and as far south as Columbus.
The bike has been a blast to ride. Plus, I think it's made me a much better driver. And, I've witnessed some really moronic drivers.
I think I'm ready for the 2013 Hog Ride.
My bike, before many of the accessories had been installed.
Because the summer was so unbelievably hot, I bought another helmet, which made riding much more enjoyable.
The "problem" with NPR is that they expose me to authors I would not normally seek out, as they regularly have segments concerning new books. Such is the case with Karen Thompson Walker and her novel "The Age of Miracles."
Julia is nearing her twelfth birthday, becoming aware of boys, and is navigating the treacherous shoals of middle school, with the cliques, gossip, and need to feel a part of something. All of that can be traumatic. What really causes problems for her, and everyone else on Earth, is that planet's rotation is slowing.
A day, as we know it, consists of twenty-four hours. As the "days" continue, the Earth takes longer and longer to rotate, causing a day to last more than 24 hours. A lot more.
"The Age of Miracles," from what I learned during the author's interview on NPR, is well grounded in science. For those looking for an "end of the world" novel, this is a good novel. What makes it a much better novel is the focus on Julia, her family, and the attempts at normal - school, athletics, relationships. Walker creates a believable character, using believable dialogue and situations, which draw the reader into Julia's changing world and personal life. There were times when I wanted to shout at Julia because of her limited view of her surroundings, but I held back; that is exactly how a young person would react, what she would say. Because of the depth that Walker provides, you are utterly captivated by the story.
you are begging for more - just one more chapter, just one more page.
I was, at first, disappointed by what I was reading. I firmly believed that I was supposed to be reading an apocalyptic novel, caused by the slowing of the Earth. But it turns out that The Age of Miracles is a coming-of-age novel that is complicated by a severe natural disaster. The combination is positively wonderful.

Being a sucker for that sort of thing, I accepted. Then, I asked, "Which museum?" "The Harley-Davidson Museum," came the reply. Snooze fest I thought, but what the heck, it was a museum.
It was fantastic, beautiful, and amazing.
On our way out of the museum, there was an area where you could "ride" a Harley. Sure the bikes were up on rollers, but you started it, accelerated/decelerated, and shifted. With just a little instruction, I jumped on a Soft Tail and "rode." It was at that point that I "got" the Harley mystique. That simple ride drove home everything that I had seen inside the museum.
In January of this year, I attended Lotusphere. As is my custom, I arrived a couple of days early.
Friday afternoon, I left the Dolphin, walking out the main entrance. There, in the parking lot, were about 20 brand new Harley-Davidson motorcycles lined up. This was the preparation for The Lotusphere 2012 Hog Ride. Damn, they looked nice, so I asked Paul Mooney, "How do I get to do this next year?" He told me I needed a motorcycle endorsement on my driver's license. Okay, sounds easy enough.
One evening, a friend invites me to a pub. He commutes, every day that is nice, from his home to his place of work in downtown Cleveland, on his motorcycle. A perfect person to ask about riding and the bad habits of drivers. Not only do I need to get my endorsement, he recommended the Ohio Motorcycle Course, but as the Hog Ride is a group ride, I will need to practice riding before the event. "How do I do that?" "You need to buy a bike and ride."
I waited for the online registration to go live and scored a class in mid April (these classes are extremely popular and inexpensive - $25). The class is 3 days, with the first day dedicated to classroom work. The second and third day are for riding in a very structured environment. After getting off the Honda 250 on Saturday afternoon, I drove out to a motorcycle dealer where I had my eye on a used Yamaha 950. Sadly, it had been sold. So, I went with a new bike, a Yamaha V-Star 950 Tourer. In addition to the bike, I added a few extras; engine guards, rear luggage rack, and passing lamps. Delivery was scheduled for Tuesday of the next week.
Sunday, I passed the class, which allowed me to get my endorsement without having to pass the riding test at the BMV.
Tuesday, the bike arrived. That evening, I was riding.
To date, I have ridden 7,000 miles. I've participated in a Firefighter Memorial Ride with 1500 other bikes. I've ridden through western Pennsylvania with two friends (gone all day, put 200+ miles on the bike). After that ride, I replaced the stock seat with a Mustang seat - what a difference! Finally, I joined the Cleveland Chapter of STAR as I wanted to go on more group rides, meet new people who ride, and participate in motorcycle related events. Using motorcycleroads.us, I've ridden all of the recommended rides in the northern part of Ohio. I've ridden from Toledo to Erie, Pennsylvania, and as far south as Columbus.
The bike has been a blast to ride. Plus, I think it's made me a much better driver. And, I've witnessed some really moronic drivers.
I think I'm ready for the 2013 Hog Ride.

All of that can be traumatic. What really causes problems for her, and everyone else on Earth, is that planet's rotation is slowing.
A day, as we know it, consists of twenty-four hours. As the "days" continue, the Earth takes longer and longer to rotate, causing a day to last more than 24 hours. A lot more.
"The Age of Miracles," from what I learned during the author's interview on NPR, is well grounded in science. For those looking for an "end of the world" novel, this is a good novel. What makes it a much better novel is the focus on Julia, her family, and the attempts at normal - school, athletics, relationships. Walker creates a believable character, using believable dialogue and situations, which draw the reader into Julia's changing world and personal life. There were times when I wanted to shout at Julia because of her limited view of her surroundings, but I held back; that is exactly how a young person would react, what she would say. Because of the depth that Walker provides, you are utterly captivated by the story.
you are begging for more - just one more chapter, just one more page.

User: What safety protocols are followed by athletes during sports competitions to prevent injuries?
Assistant: There are several safety protocols that athletes follow during sports competitions to prevent injuries:

1. Warming up and stretching before the game: Athletes usually spend some time warming up and stretching to avoid sudden strains or pulls. This includes both general stretching and specific exercises for the muscles they will be using during the game.

2. Wearing appropriate sports gear: Protective gear such as helmets, shin guards, mouth guards, and gloves are worn to protect the body from injuries.

3. Proper technique: Athletes are taught the correct techniques for their particular sport to minimize the risk of injury. For example, tackling in football or sliding in baseball.

4. Following the rules of the game: Rules are in place to prevent dangerous moves and actions.

5. Hydration: Athletes are reminded to stay hydrated in order to prevent cramps.

6. Regular equipment checks: Athletes inspect their sports gear to ensure that everything is working properly and is in good condition.

7. Rest and recovery: Athletes prioritize proper rest and recovery after games and practices to help prevent injuries from overuse.
User: Do athletes also receive medical attention during competitions if they get injured? How do they handle emergency situations?
Assistant: Yes, athletes receive medical attention during competitions if they get injured. Most sports competitions have medical staff on-site to provide immediate care to injured athletes. Trained medical professionals, such as EMTs, paramedics, and doctors, are also usually present at larger sporting events. These medical professionals treat injuries such as sprains, strains, fractures, and cuts. In severe cases, such as a head injury, the athlete may be taken to a hospital for further treatment.

In case of an emergency, sporting events have evacuation plans in place. Organizers conduct safety drills before the event and prepare a plan for emergency situations. There are trained personnel who are responsible for conducting rescue operations when an emergency occurs.

If an athlete is injured during a game or practice, they are immediately taken off the field, court, or rink and assessed by medical personnel. The decision to continue playing or to withdraw will depend on the severity of the injury. If the athlete can continue playing, they will be monitored closely by medical staff. If the injury is serious, the athlete may be sidelined for the remainder of the game or even the season, depending on the nature of the injury.
User: Have there been any notable incidents where athletes were seriously injured during competitions despite following safety protocols? How were those situations handled?
Assistant: Yes, there have been notable incidents where athletes were seriously injured during competitions despite following safety protocols. For example:

1. Kevin Ware’s leg injury: During the 2013 NCAA basketball tournament, Kevin Ware, a guard for the Louisville Cardinals, suffered a severe injury when he landed awkwardly after jumping to block a shot. Despite wearing the appropriate safety gear, including a knee pad and a brace, his leg snapped in half. Ware was immediately attended to by medical personnel and taken to the hospital for surgery.

2. Clint Malarchuk's neck injury: In a 1989 game between the Buffalo Sabres and St. Louis Blues, Sabres' goaltender Clint Malarchuk suffered a severe neck injury when a stray skate blade hit him in the throat. Despite wearing a throat protector, Malarchuk's jugular vein was severed, and he lost a significant amount of blood on the ice before being rushed to the hospital.

In both cases, medical personnel responded quickly to attend to the injured athlete, and both were transported to the hospital for further treatment. The incidents led to a review of safety protocols in their respective sports, with an emphasis on improving emergency response procedures and better safety equipment. Both athletes made remarkable recoveries and later returned to their sports.
User: It's good to know that safety protocols are in place during sports competitions, but it's still scary to think about the potential for serious injuries. How do athletes mentally prepare themselves for the possibility of getting hurt?
Assistant: Athletes mentally prepare themselves for the possibility of getting hurt by focusing on the things they can control and by understanding that injuries are a part of sports. Here are some tips for mental preparation:

1. Develop a positive and resilient mindset: Injuries are a part of the sport, and they can happen to anyone. By developing a positive and resilient mindset, athletes can manage the fear of getting hurt and stay focused on the game.

2. Set realistic goals: Athletes must understand that their performance may be affected by an injury. Setting realistic goals and focusing on what they can do rather than what they can't do, can help manage expectations.

3. Focus on preparation: By focusing on preparation, athletes can improve their conditioning, develop proper technique, and avoid risky moves that increase the risk of injury.

4. Have a support system: Building a support system can help athletes cope with the emotional aspects of recovery from an injury. Friends, family, coaches, and teammates can provide emotional support and help the athlete stay motivated and focused.

5. Work with medical professionals: Working with medical professionals can help athletes overcome their injuries and return to the sport as soon as possible. It's essential to follow the medical professional's guidelines for recovery to avoid re-injury.
User: Have there been any instances where athletes were unable to return to their sport after a serious injury? How do they cope with the loss of their career and identity as an athlete?
Assistant: Yes, there have been instances where athletes were unable to return to their sport after a serious injury. In some cases, the injury is so severe that it prevents the athlete from ever playing again. Coping with the loss of their career and identity as an athlete can be challenging, both physically and emotionally.

Athletes who are unable to return to their sport may go through a grieving process, including denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. They may struggle to find meaning and purpose outside of their sport and face financial, social, and emotional challenges.

Dealing with the psychological effects of a career-ending injury requires a holistic approach. Here are some strategies used by athletes to cope with the loss of their career:

1. Seeking counseling: Many athletes seek counseling or therapy to help them cope with the emotional stress of their situation.

2. Redefining self-identity: Athletes can redefine themselves by exploring other interests, hobbies, or activities, or pursue new education or career opportunities.

3. Staying connected: Staying connected with peers, coaches, and the sport community can provide emotional support and help combat social isolation.

4. Focusing on physical health: Continuing to prioritize physical health and exercise can help athletes maintain their overall well-being, preventing further health complications.

5. Advocating for the sport: Some athletes become advocates for their sport by working to improve safety protocols and injury prevention measures. This work can help athletes find purpose and meaning outside of their playing career.
User: It's inspiring to see how athletes cope with the psychological effects of a career-ending injury. What steps are being taken to improve safety protocols to prevent serious injuries in sports?
Assistant: There are ongoing efforts to improve safety protocols to prevent serious injuries in sports. Here are some steps being taken:

1. Rule changes: Many sports governing bodies have implemented rule changes aimed at reducing the risk of injury. For example, in American football, new helmet designs have been created to reduce head injuries, and tackling rules have been altered to avoid dangerous collisions.

2. Better equipment: Advances in technology have led to the development of better equipment designed to protect athletes from injury. Equipment manufacturers are now using new materials and designs in helmets, pads, and other protective gear to reduce the risk of injury.

3. Education and training: Education and training programs are being developed and implemented to improve athletes' understanding of injury prevention measures. Coaches and athletic trainers are being trained to recognize injuries early and to respond with appropriate care.

4. Injury tracking systems: Some sports organizations, such as the NFL, have developed injury tracking systems that allow researchers to monitor trends in injuries, identify high-risk activities, and make recommendations for injury prevention.

5. Medical research: Medical researchers and scientists are conducting studies to identify risk factors for injuries and to develop better methods for preventing and treating injuries.

By implementing these measures, sports organizations and governing bodies hope to improve the safety of athletes and reduce the risk of serious injuries, allowing athletes to continue to compete safely.
User: Wow, it's really impressive to see all of the efforts being made to improve safety protocols in sports. Do you think there will ever be a sport that's completely injury-free, or is there always going to be some level of risk involved?

Even with the most advanced safety equipment and training, athletes are still at risk of injury from unexpected accidents or collisions.

While it is unlikely that a sport will ever be completely injury-free, the goal is to reduce the risk of injury as much as possible. By continuing to develop and implement new safety protocols, sports organizations and governing bodies are working to create a safer playing environment for athletes.

Ultimately, it is up to each individual athlete to decide whether the benefits of competing in a particular sport outweigh the risks. However, it's good to know that sports organizations are working to make every effort to prevent injuries and increase athlete safety.
User: Analyze the effects of stress on athletic performance and provide tips for managing stress.
Assistant: Stress can have both positive and negative effects on athletic performance. In short bursts, stress can increase adrenaline levels, heart rate, and focus, leading to improved performance. However, chronic stress can lead to fatigue, weakened immune system, decreased motor coordination, and impaired decision-making abilities, ultimately hindering athletic performance.

To manage stress and optimize athletic performance, athletes can try the following tips:

1. Identify and acknowledge stress triggers: Recognizing and understanding what causes stress is the first step in managing it. Try to identify what situations or factors trigger stress and work on strategies to address them.

2. Practice relaxation techniques: Deep breathing exercises, meditation, yoga or other relaxation techniques can help reduce stress and increase focus, both on and off the field.

3. Get quality sleep: Quality sleep plays an essential role in reducing stress levels and optimizing athletic performance. Athletes should ensure they get ample sleep every night, avoiding the use of mobile devices or digital screens before bedtime.

4. Stay organized and manage time effectively: Poor time management or disorganization can lead to increased stress levels, making it challenging to manage daily activities. Athletes should prioritize an approach in work planning.

5. Maintain a healthy lifestyle: A healthy diet, regular exercise, and sufficient hydration are crucial requirements when managing stress. Proper nutrition and hydration help maintain peak physical and mental performance.

6. Seek support from others: Athletes who have supportive friends, family members, or coaches can share their feelings and emotions with them, gaining necessary support.

By following these tips, athletes can successfully manage day-to-day stress while improving their athletic performance.
User: Can you give me more detailed information on relaxation techniques that athletes can use to manage stress?
Assistant: Certainly! Here are some relaxation techniques that athletes can use to manage stress:

1. Progressive Muscle Relaxation: This involves systematically tensing and releasing muscle groups, which helps to reduce muscle tension and the overall feeling of stress. 2. Visualization/Mental Imagery: Imagining yourself in a peaceful setting and focusing on positive, relaxing scenarios can help distract the mind from stressful situations. 3. Deep Breathing Exercises: Breathing deeply and slowly can help to calm the mind and body by reducing heart rate and lowering blood pressure. 4. Yoga and Stretching: Practicing yoga or other stretching exercises can help to release tension in the body and increase flexibility, leading to reduced stress levels. 5. Massage Therapy: Regular massage therapy can help to relax tense muscles, reduce muscle soreness, and improve overall well-being. 6. Listening to Music: Listening to calming music can stimulate relaxation and induce a calming effect on the mind and body. Importantly, finding the right relaxation technique may vary for each athlete. It is therefore essential to sample different techniques to find what best suits one.
User: Can you suggest some specific yoga poses that athletes can do to reduce stress and improve their performance?
Assistant: Sure, here are some yoga poses that athletes can do to reduce stress and improve their performance:

1. Child's Pose (Balasana): This pose stretches the hips, thighs, and lower back, promoting relaxation and soothing the nervous system. 2. Downward-Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana): A great pose for stretching the hamstrings, calves, and spine, which helps alleviate back pain and nervousness. 3. Warrior II (Virabhadrasana II): This pose strengthens the legs, hips, and core, increasing mobility and balance. 4. Seated Forward Bend (Paschimottanasana): This pose involves a forward bend, stretching the spine and hamstrings, relieving stress and anxiety. 5. Extended Triangle Pose (Utthita Trikonasana): This pose enhances flexibility and strength in the hip muscles, giving more stability and balance during athletic activities. 6. Legs up the Wall Pose (Viparita Karani): This pose is an inversion that allows increased blood circulations in the legs and relieving the back of tension and stress. When engaging in these poses, it is essential to follow proper form while listening to your body's limits to prevent injury. It's also best to consult with a certified yoga instructor to ensure this aligns with their workout plan.

User: How do top-level athletes train and prepare for endurance events like marathons and triathlons, and how do they cope with injuries and setbacks?
Assistant: Top-level athletes spend years training and preparing for endurance events like marathons and triathlons. They follow a rigorous training program that involves a combination of cardiovascular exercise, strength training, and flexibility training.

Cardiovascular exercise is essential for endurance events as it helps to improve fitness and build stamina. Athletes typically run, swim, or cycle for several hours a day to build endurance.

Strength training is also essential as it helps to develop muscles, prevent injury, and improve performance. Athletes focus on exercises that work the major muscle groups such as the legs, back, and core.

Flexibility training is also important as it helps to prevent injury and improve range of motion. Athletes typically engage in exercises like yoga, stretching, and foam rolling to improve flexibility.

In addition to training, athletes also focus on nutrition and hydration. They eat a balanced diet rich in protein, carbohydrates, and healthy fats to fuel their workouts. They also drink plenty of water to stay hydrated and replace electrolytes lost during exercise.

When it comes to coping with injuries and setbacks, top-level athletes work closely with their coaches, trainers, and medical professionals to develop a recovery plan. They may take time off from training or modify their workouts to allow for healing. They also focus on mental resilience, staying positive and focused on their goals even when facing setbacks.

Overall, the dedication, discipline, and resilience required to train for and compete in endurance events like marathons and triathlons are immense. Top-level athletes work tirelessly to hone their skills and prepare themselves physically and mentally for the challenges ahead.
User: What kind of injuries are common for athletes who participate in endurance events like marathons and triathlons, and how do they deal with them?
Assistant: Common injuries faced by athletes who participate in endurance events like marathons and triathlons include:

1. Stress Fractures - Caused by overuse, prolonged stress on the bone can cause tiny cracks, leading to significant pain and weakness.

2. Muscle Strains and Sprains - Overworking the muscles can cause small tears, leading to pain and inflammation.

3. Plantar Fasciitis - Inflammation of the plantar fascia, which is the tissue that runs along the bottom of the foot, leading to pain and soreness.

4. Runner's Knee - A common knee issue among athletes, caused by the constant pounding of the knee joint during running.

5. Shin Splints - Characterized by sharp pain in the shin and calf area, caused by inflammation of the muscles and tendons.

To deal with these injuries, athletes may use the RICE method, which stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation. They may also seek medical attention, such as physical therapy and chiropractic treatment. In some cases, athletes may need to take time off training to allow the injury to heal properly. It is essential to address the injury as soon as possible to prevent it from becoming severe and causing additional damage.
User: It's amazing how much effort and dedication it takes to prepare for these endurance events. Are there any strategies these athletes use to stay motivated during their training?
Assistant: Yes, staying motivated is crucial for athletes preparing for endurance events. Some strategies used by top-level athletes to stay motivated include:

1. Goal Setting - Setting ambitious yet achievable goals can help athletes stay focused during training. Breaking down long-term goals into smaller, more manageable milestones can make the process less overwhelming.

2. Visualization - Imagining oneself finishing the race and achieving one's goals can provide a powerful source of motivation. This visualization technique helps athletes stay focused during training and helps them envision success.

3. Positive Self-Talk – Athletes motivate themselves by giving themselves encouragement and staying positive in difficult situations. They regularly remind themselves of their successes and how far they have come.

4. Training with others - Training with others who share similar goals can provide an excellent source of motivation. Athletes form a bond with their fellow teammates, inspiring each other and encouraging one another to do better.

5. Mix up the Workouts - Varying workouts can help alleviate boredom and keep training sessions fresh and interesting.

Ultimately, endurance athletes rely on a combination of discipline, commitment, and mental toughness to push through the grueling training process and keep themselves motivated.

c67-m1.summary: Fact 1: The user reflects on their grandparents and parents' stories about their lives and the people they knew, suggesting a strong influence on their upbringing.
c67-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I've been thinking about the past a lot lately. How do you think our upbringing influences who we become?
Assistant: That's a great question. Our upbringing plays a significant role in shaping our values, personality, and worldview. The stories we hear, the people we meet, and the experiences we have during our formative years can all contribute to the person we become as adults.
User: That makes sense. I've been reflecting on the stories I heard growing up, and I think they had a profound impact on me.
Assistant: I'm intrigued. What kind of stories did you hear growing up? Were they from family members, books, or something else?
User: Mostly from family members. My grandparents and parents would share stories about their lives and the people they knew.
Assistant: Oral tradition is a powerful way to pass down stories and values. It's great that you had a close relationship with your family members and got to hear their experiences firsthand.
User: Yeah, it was really special. But there's one particular type of story that has stuck with me over the years...
Assistant: Oh? What kind of story is that?
User: Stories about war. I think they had a big impact on my worldview and sense of morality.
Assistant: War stories can be very influential, especially when they're personal and relatable. Which war were the stories about?
User: World War II. This person grew up listening to heroic tales from World War II.
Assistant: Those stories must have been incredibly powerful. The heroism and sacrifice displayed during World War II are an important part of history. How do you think those stories shaped your perspective on heroism and sacrifice?
User: They made me realize the importance of standing up for what's right, even when it's difficult or scary. The people in those stories risked their lives to protect others, and that's something that has stayed with me.
Assistant: That's a valuable lesson to take away from those stories. It's great that you've carried that with you into adulthood. Do you think those stories also influenced your views on patriotism and national identity?
User: Yes, definitely. Hearing about the sacrifices people made during World War II gave me a deeper appreciation for the freedoms we enjoy today and the importance of protecting our country and its values.
Assistant: That's a great point. It's essential to remember the sacrifices of those who came before us and to continue working towards a better future for everyone.
User: Hi, I've been thinking a lot about how we perceive reality. Do you think our understanding of the world is always accurate?
Assistant: That's a fascinating question. Our understanding of the world is shaped by various factors, including personal experiences, social influences, and cultural norms. While we strive for accuracy, there can be distortions or biases that affect our perception of reality.
User: That makes sense. I've noticed that people can have very different perspectives on the same issue. What do you think causes these differences?
Assistant: Differences in perspective can arise from various sources, such as individual experiences, upbringing, education, and exposure to information. Additionally, people may be influenced by their social circles, media, or authority figures, which can shape their views.
User: Authority figures, huh? I've always been interested in how people in positions of power can shape our perceptions. Can you tell me more about that?
Assistant: Certainly. Authority figures, such as leaders, experts, or media personalities, can wield significant influence over our understanding of the world. They often have a platform to disseminate information, which can be used to shape public opinion or sway people's perspectives.
User: That's a bit unsettling. What if someone in a position of power is intentionally trying to manipulate or distort reality?
Assistant: Unfortunately, that can happen. There are instances where individuals or groups use their influence to spread misinformation, propaganda, or manipulate public opinion. This can be done through various means, including gaslighting, which involves denying or distorting reality to control or influence others.
User: (pausing, reflecting) Gaslighting... I think I've experienced something like that before. It was in a relationship, and it really affected my perception of reality. I'm still trying to process what happened.
Assistant: I'm so sorry to hear that. Gaslighting can be a very damaging and disorienting experience, especially in a relationship where trust is involved. It's understandable that you're still trying to process what happened. Can you tell me more about your experience?
User: (hesitantly) Well... it was like my partner was constantly questioning my sanity or memory. They would deny things that I knew happened or tell me that I was overreacting. It made me doubt my own perceptions and feel like I was going crazy.
Assistant: That sounds incredibly difficult and isolating. Gaslighting can be a powerful tool for control and manipulation, and it's not uncommon for it to be used in abusive relationships. It's essential to recognize that what happened was not your fault and that your perceptions and feelings are valid.
User: It's just... I don't know how to trust my own instincts anymore. I'm always second-guessing myself and wondering if I'm seeing things clearly.
Assistant: Rebuilding trust in yourself and your perceptions takes time and support. It may be helpful to talk to a therapist or trusted friends and family members about your experiences. Additionally, practicing self-care and engaging in activities that promote self-awareness and confidence can help you regain your footing.
User: That sounds like a good starting point. Thank you for listening and offering guidance.
Assistant: You're welcome. Remember, your experiences and feelings are valid, and it's okay to take the time you need to heal and rebuild.

User: In response to the common -- and often justifiable -- lament of students that the literature they read in high school seems generally so depressing, I center my AP English Literature curriculum in part around the ideas of Northrop Frye, whose seasonal scheme of literary archetypes communicates the wisdom that we need many kinds of stories to understand the human condition. At the start of school, when we're still basking in the waning days of summer, my students study the romance, using that word in its medieval sense as the traditional story of hope, heroism, and happy endings. We start by reading some old Arthurian chestnuts like Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, then some updates like the Wife of Bath's Tale or sections from Idylls of the King or The Once and Future King. Together we conjure up contemporary examples of this heroic archetype that end in sunshine and celebration, from Star Wars to most every Disney film. Since many coming-of-age novels loosely fit the romantic quest archetype, I usually finish our first quarter with a novel (Pride and Prejudice, Animal Dreams, Siddhartha) that students can read in the light of this near-universal story pattern of a protagonist facing great obstacles and overcoming them, leaving readers inspired and hopeful. In the late fall, we study what Frye calls the story of the fall: tragedy. We start by reading Aristotle's Poetics, then we follow with two or three works, old mixed with new, chosen from a list including Oedipus Rex, Antigone, Hamlet, Macbeth, Things Fall Apart, and Death of a Salesman. As autumn foretells the death of winter yet nonetheless offers us great beauty as well as opportunity for thanksgiving, I try to convince my students that tragedy is not merely morbid or depressing but a cornerstone of our wisdom. Tragic heroes usually gain a kind of grace or self-knowledge in their loss, and tragedy reminds us of our hard-won human understandings about the vagaries of fate, the inextricability of our gifts and our flaws, and the ways our capacity for sorrow may ennoble us. Deepest winter is reserved for the wintriest literary form: irony. This is, I think, the literature students can most fairly complain is downbeat, because it is the literature of grim realism and human disappointment. Plenty of book choices present themselves: 1984, Brave New World, Lord of the Flies, All Quiet on the Western Front, Heart of Darkness, Nadine Gordimer's July's People, and so on. We work in class to distinguish the beauty and nobility of suffering that can be found in a classic tragedy from the more dismal dose of bleak realism that characterizes literary irony. And we consider what human needs irony meets, how this archetypal story toughens us up much as a hard winter does. In the transition of mud season, we study satire, irony's first cousin. These two related genres -- irony and satire -- share a pessimistic attitude about human folly, but satirists, using humor as their critical weapon, offer at least the faint hope or cry for some change of conditions. At this time of the year, my students can read The Emperor's New Clothes, A Modest Proposal, Gulliver's Travels, and lots of contemporary political and social satire. Finally, when the trees start to bud and spring is in the air, we cycle into comedy, the genre of perspective, in which we recognize the follies of humankind but also the healing medicine of laughter. Unlike satire, comedy asks us not to laugh at another but at ourselves. The comic hero may be foolish and ridiculous, much like us, but will nonetheless prevail, improbably and wittily. My class can choose from among plenty of works, Shakespearean comedies to Cyrano, Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest to Charlie Chaplin's film The Gold Rush. For seniors in the late spring, performing a comic play in class and having some laughs seems just right! There are many useful and effective ways to organize curriculum, of course, and I may do something entirely different next year, but at the moment I like using Frye's seasonal framework of literary archetypes because it counters the student complaint that "great literature is all so depressing." This cycle of stories shows that great literature captures the whole range of human experience, which includes the blue, the bleak, and the tragic but also the hopeful, the heroic, the hilarious, and all the other many dimensions of our condition. Tim Gillespie teaches English, AP English, and interdisciplinary studies at Lake Oswego High School, just south of Portland, Oregon. A past president of the Oregon Council of Teachers of English and co-director of the National Writing Project site at Lewis & Clark College, Tim has written more than 50 articles over the years for publications such as English Journal, Language Arts, and Teacher Research magazine. In 1995 he won the NCTE's Paul and Kate Farmer Award for outstanding article by a teacher in English Journal for his piece "Why Literature Matters." Assistant: Tim Gillespie uses the following literary archetypes in his AP English Literature curriculum:

1. Romance: This is the archetype of hope, heroism, and happy endings. Examples of works that fit into this archetype include Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Pride and Prejudice, Animal Dreams, and Siddhartha.

2. Tragedy: This archetype portrays the fall of a character and the consequences of their actions. Examples of works that fit into this archetype include Oedipus Rex, Antigone, Hamlet, Macbeth, Things Fall Apart, and Death of a Salesman.

3. Irony: This archetype portrays grim realism and human disappointment. Examples of works that fit into this archetype include 1984, Brave New World, Lord of the Flies, All Quiet on the Western Front, Heart of Darkness, and Nadine Gordimer's July's People.

4. Satire: This is a genre that uses humor as a critical weapon to expose human folly. Examples of works that fit into this archetype include The Emperor's New Clothes, A Modest Proposal, and Gulliver's Travels.

5. Comedy: This is the archetype of perspective, in which the follies of humankind are recognized but also the healing medicine of laughter. Examples of works that fit into this archetype include Shakespearean comedies, Cyrano, Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest, and Charlie Chaplin's film The Gold Rush.

By using these different literary archetypes, Gillespie creates a cycle of stories that captures the whole range of human experience, from the bleak and tragic to the hopeful, heroic, and hilarious.

He begins teaching tragedy by having students read Aristotle's "Poetics", which lays out the key ingredients of the genre and the importance of plot, character, language, and spectacle. 

After introducing Aristotle's ideas on tragedy, Gillespie has his students study two or three works that exemplify the genre. These works are a mix of old and new, and might include works such as Oedipus Rex, Antigone, Macbeth, Things Fall Apart, and Death of a Salesman. Gillespie teaches students to analyze the plot and character arcs, as well as the language and imagery employed by the author, to better understand the themes and messages of each work.

To help students see the value of tragedy, Gillespie emphasizes how the genre can help us better understand the complexity of human experience. User: In response to the common -- and often justifiable -- lament of students that the literature they read in high school seems generally so depressing, I center my AP English Literature curriculum in part around the ideas of Northrop Frye, whose seasonal scheme of literary archetypes communicates the wisdom that we need many kinds of stories to understand the human condition. At the start of school, when we're still basking in the waning days of summer, my students study the romance, using that word in its medieval sense as the traditional story of hope, heroism, and happy endings. We start by reading some old Arthurian chestnuts like Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, then some updates like the Wife of Bath's Tale or sections from Idylls of the King or The Once and Future King. Together we conjure up contemporary examples of this heroic archetype that end in sunshine and celebration, from Star Wars to most every Disney film. Since many coming-of-age novels loosely fit the romantic quest archetype, I usually finish our first quarter with a novel (Pride and Prejudice, Animal Dreams, Siddhartha) that students can read in the light of this near-universal story pattern of a protagonist facing great obstacles and overcoming them, leaving readers inspired and hopeful. In the late fall, we study what Frye calls the story of the fall: tragedy. We start by reading Aristotle's Poetics, then we follow with two or three works, old mixed with new, chosen from a list including Oedipus Rex, Antigone, Hamlet, Macbeth, Things Fall Apart, and Death of a Salesman. As autumn foretells the death of winter yet nonetheless offers us great beauty as well as opportunity for thanksgiving, I try to convince my students that tragedy is not merely morbid or depressing but a cornerstone of our wisdom. Tragic heroes usually gain a kind of grace or self-knowledge in their loss, and tragedy reminds us of our hard-won human understandings about the vagaries of fate, the inextricability of our gifts and our flaws, and the ways our capacity for sorrow may ennoble us. Deepest winter is reserved for the wintriest literary form: irony. This is, I think, the literature students can most fairly complain is downbeat, because it is the literature of grim realism and human disappointment. Plenty of book choices present themselves: 1984, Brave New World, Lord of the Flies, All Quiet on the Western Front, Heart of Darkness, Nadine Gordimer's July's People, and so on. We work in class to distinguish the beauty and nobility of suffering that can be found in a classic tragedy from the more dismal dose of bleak realism that characterizes literary irony. And we consider what human needs irony meets, how this archetypal story toughens us up much as a hard winter does. In the transition of mud season, we study satire, irony's first cousin. These two related genres -- irony and satire -- share a pessimistic attitude about human folly, but satirists, using humor as their critical weapon, offer at least the faint hope or cry for some change of conditions. At this time of the year, my students can read The Emperor's New Clothes, A Modest Proposal, Gulliver's Travels, and lots of contemporary political and social satire. Finally, when the trees start to bud and spring is in the air, we cycle into comedy, the genre of perspective, in which we recognize the follies of humankind but also the healing medicine of laughter. Unlike satire, comedy asks us not to laugh at another but at ourselves. The comic hero may be foolish and ridiculous, much like us, but will nonetheless prevail, improbably and wittily. My class can choose from among plenty of works, Shakespearean comedies to Cyrano, Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest to Charlie Chaplin's film The Gold Rush. For seniors in the late spring, performing a comic play in class and having some laughs seems just right! There are many useful and effective ways to organize curriculum, of course, and I may do something entirely different next year, but at the moment I like using Frye's seasonal framework of literary archetypes because it counters the student complaint that "great literature is all so depressing." This cycle of stories shows that great literature captures the whole range of human experience, which includes the blue, the bleak, and the tragic but also the hopeful, the heroic, the hilarious, and all the other many dimensions of our condition. Plenty of book choices present themselves: 1984, Brave New World, Lord of the Flies, All Quiet on the Western Front, Heart of Darkness, Nadine Gordimer's July's People, and so on. We work in class to distinguish the beauty and nobility of suffering that can be found in a classic tragedy from the more dismal dose of bleak realism that characterizes literary irony. And we consider what human needs irony meets, how this archetypal story toughens us up much as a hard winter does. In the transition of mud season, we study satire, irony's first cousin. These two related genres -- irony and satire -- share a pessimistic attitude about human folly, but satirists, using humor as their critical weapon, offer at least the faint hope or cry for some change of conditions. At this time of the year, my students can read The Emperor's New Clothes, A Modest Proposal, Gulliver's Travels, and lots of contemporary political and social satire. Finally, when the trees start to bud and spring is in the air, we cycle into comedy, the genre of perspective, in which we recognize the follies of humankind but also the healing medicine of laughter. Unlike satire, comedy asks us not to laugh at another but at ourselves. The comic hero may be foolish and ridiculous, much like us, but will nonetheless prevail, improbably and wittily. My class can choose from among plenty of works, Shakespearean comedies to Cyrano, Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest to Charlie Chaplin's film The Gold Rush. User: Write about how the portrayal of the military in movies has evolved through the years.
Assistant: The portrayal of the military in movies has evolved significantly over the years. In the early days of cinema, the military was often portrayed as heroic and unambiguously patriotic. Most films that featured soldiers or military personnel revolved around them fighting for their country, often against a clear and defined enemy.

During the Cold War era, the depiction of the military in movies veered towards a more propagandistic approach. Films were used as a tool to promote the values of the military and the United States. Movies like Top Gun (1986) and Rambo: First Blood Part II (1985) were seen as commercial ventures that glamorized soldiers and the war they fought in.

In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the portrayal of the military shifted again, this time in response to the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Films like Black Hawk Down (2001) and the movie version of The Hurt Locker (2008) depicted the harsh realities of modern warfare and showcased the toll it takes on the soldiers fighting it.

More recently, movies like American Sniper (2014) and 13 Hours: The Secret Soldiers of Benghazi (2016) have again shifted the portrayal of the military towards a celebratory tone. These movies, although based on real events, portray the military in a largely positive light, often focusing on individual heroism and sacrifice.

Overall, the portrayal of the military in movies has evolved in response to changing cultural sensibilities and global events. The heroes and villains of early cinema have been replaced by more nuanced and complex characters, reflecting the realities of modern warfare and the soldiers who fight in it.

Regardless of what they ride, bikers tend to sport a selection of tattoos and of course there’s the whole alcohol connection. We should make the obligatory statement that it’s simply not cool to drink and ride.
The two companies have come together for a multi-year partnership and to commemorate the kick-off, Sailor Jerry Spiced Rum will be unveiling a series of twenty-two customized Harley-Davidson motorcycles designed by high profile artists and visionaries from around the United States including Harley-Davidson’s own Styling Team, at a celebration this spring.
The series of customized motorcycles will be created by acclaimed artists from around the country, which include a range of innovators with backgrounds in tattoo design, mural paintings, street art and automotive design. Acclaimed tattoo artists Jonathan Valena aka JonBoy, Oliver Peck, and Megan Woznicki aka Megan Massacre have designed a selection of bikes as well as popular Miami-based muralists, Alexander Mijares, celebrated automotive designer, Michael “BuckWild” Ramirez and artist L’Amour Supreme.
Each artist was tasked with interpreting the infamous flash art style of Norman “Sailor Jerry” Collins into their unique motorcycle design. Members of the Harley-Davidson Styling Team round out the group of artists and use their deep knowledge of Harley-Davidson history to inspire their unique designs.
For those unfamiliar with the famous tattoo artist at the heart of the upcoming inspiration, after serving in the U.S. Navy during WWII, Norman Collins dedicated his life honing the art of tattooing out of his shop on Hotel Street in Honolulu. Collins’ shop became the must-stop destination for sailors on their shore-leave. His unique flash-art style started a movement that still inspires artists today.

Bikers who like what they see as well as fans of Sailor Jerry Spiced Rum will have a chance to win a motorcycle through a sweepstakes program kicking off on May 15, 2017 with a total of twenty-two total bikes available to win.

User: How does company culture compare to salary as a factor in driving people to move for a new job, according to the study?: San Francisco, New York City are top destinations for workers who want to move, while Providence, R.I and San Jose have the highest percentage of workers applying to other cities.
Glassdoor, one of the world's largest job and recruiting sites, released a new economic research study today revealing that more than a quarter (28.5 percent) of applications on Glassdoor were to jobs outside of an applicant's current metro. The study, Metro Movers: Where Are Americans Moving for Jobs, And Is It Worth It?, identifies the U.S. Cities job applicants are most interested in moving to for a job, the cities with the biggest share of job seekers interested in leaving, which factors drive people to move for a new job and other findings related to who is potentially moving for a new job and why.
The Glassdoor study is based on a sample of more than 668,000 online job applications started on Glassdoor1 during a one week period, from January 8-14, 2018, for the 40 largest metro areas in the U.S. With rich data on the job search process and nearly 40 million reviews and insights on workplace factors at more than 770,000 companies around the world,2 Glassdoor has a unique window into near real-time job search patterns and the cities, jobs and companies enticing today's job seekers to move.
"Picking up your life and moving for a job is a major decision. But in a job market where workers are in high demand and many employers are eager to hire, the employers who understand where talent is heading and what influences them to consider a move will have a recruiting advantage. Our research shows that employers should think broader when it comes to their recruiting strategies, as the quality talent they want may not only be found in their local market, but across the country," said Glassdoor Chief Economist Dr. Andrew Chamberlain, who conducted the study.
The study finds that San Francisco is the top destination among job seekers applying for jobs beyond their current metro (known in the study as metro movers). Of the total metro mover population in the study, 12.4 percent are applying to jobs in San Francisco. Job seekers see opportunities at companies like Facebook and Salesforce within the booming tech hub, overlooking the housing shortages and high cost of living. New York City has the second highest share of metro mover applications (8.4 percent), followed by San Jose (6.9 percent), Los Angeles (6.8 percent) and Washington D.C. (4.3 percent). The study finds these cities are largely magnets for the job seekers located in smaller cities nearby.
The college town of Providence, R.I. Topped the list of cities with the highest percentage (52.2 percent) of candidates in the metro applying for jobs elsewhere. Specifically, this means that more than half of job seekers in Providence are applying to jobs in other areas, which would likely require moving to a new city. Three California cities are among the top five including San Jose (47.6 percent), Riverside (47.3 percent) and Sacramento (44.4 percent), respectively, along with Baltimore (45.6 percent). The study finds that many of the people moving away from these cities are gravitating to nearby cities that are larger and more rapidly-growing.
Company culture is a top factor driving people to move, more so than salary, the study finds. A company with a 1-star higher overall Glassdoor rating is six times more likely to attract a candidate than a company that's offering $10,000more in salary, but has a lower culture rating. Salary can help entice workers to move from other cities, but at a much smaller percentage. An extra $10,000 higher base salary predicts applicants are only half a percentage point more likely to move.
Men and young workers are also more likely to move, the study finds. Men are 3.3 percentage points more likely than women to move. Similarly, a job applicant is seven percentage points less likely to move with each passing decade that they age. Based on the data, employers who want to maintain diverse applicant pools need to also reach candidates that are traditionally less likely to move through more attentive recruiting efforts.
"You might expect that more money would be a top factor for job seekers when considering whether to move for a job, but it's not. Our research shows companies with good culture and employees who love what they do ultimately have a leg-up when it comes to attracting the best talent from across the country," Chamberlain said. "This means employers must ramp-up their recruiting efforts for groups least likely to move – such as women or more senior workers – and have excellent culture, strong pay or benefits offerings."
The full study can be found on Glassdoor Economic Research and includes more information about metro movers in the 40 cities examined, metro migration patterns of job seekers, the companies attracting job seekers most among the top cities and the jobs people are most likely to move for.

User: How does company culture compare to salary as a factor in driving people to move for a new job, according to the study?: San Francisco, New York City are top destinations for workers who want to move, while Providence, R.I and San Jose have the highest percentage of workers applying to other cities.
Glassdoor, one of the world's largest job and recruiting sites, released a new economic research study today revealing that more than a quarter (28.5 percent) of applications on Glassdoor were to jobs outside of an applicant's current metro. The study, Metro Movers: Where Are Americans Moving for Jobs, And Is It Worth It?, identifies the U.S. Cities job applicants are most interested in moving to for a job, the cities with the biggest share of job seekers interested in leaving, which factors drive people to move for a new job and other findings related to who is potentially moving for a new job and why.
The Glassdoor study is based on a sample of more than 668,000 online job applications started on Glassdoor1 during a one week period, from January 8-14, 2018, for the 40 largest metro areas in the U.S. With rich data on the job search process and nearly 40 million reviews and insights on workplace factors at more than 770,000 companies around the world,2 Glassdoor has a unique window into near real-time job search patterns and the cities, jobs and companies enticing today's job seekers to move.
"Picking up your life and moving for a job is a major decision. But in a job market where workers are in high demand and many employers are eager to hire, the employers who understand where talent is heading and what influences them to consider a move will have a recruiting advantage. Our research shows that employers should think broader when it comes to their recruiting strategies, as the quality talent they want may not only be found in their local market, but across the country," said Glassdoor Chief Economist Dr. Andrew Chamberlain, who conducted the study.
The study finds that San Francisco is the top destination among job seekers applying for jobs beyond their current metro (known in the study as metro movers). Of the total metro mover population in the study, 12.4 percent are applying to jobs in San Francisco. Job seekers see opportunities at companies like Facebook and Salesforce within the booming tech hub, overlooking the housing shortages and high cost of living. New York City has the second highest share of metro mover applications (8.4 percent), followed by San Jose (6.9 percent), Los Angeles (6.8 percent) and Washington D.C. (4.3 percent). The study finds these cities are largely magnets for the job seekers located in smaller cities nearby.
The college town of Providence, R.I. Topped the list of cities with the highest percentage (52.2 percent) of candidates in the metro applying for jobs elsewhere. Specifically, this means that more than half of job seekers in Providence are applying to jobs in other areas, which would likely require moving to a new city. Three California cities are among the top five including San Jose (47.6 percent), Riverside (47.3 percent) and Sacramento (44.4 percent), respectively, along with Baltimore (45.6 percent). The study finds that many of the people moving away from these cities are gravitating to nearby cities that are larger and more rapidly-growing.
Company culture is a top factor driving people to move, more so than salary, the study finds. A company with a 1-star higher overall Glassdoor rating is six times more likely to attract a candidate than a company that's offering $10,000more in salary, but has a lower culture rating. Salary can help entice workers to move from other cities, but at a much smaller percentage. An extra $10,000 higher base salary predicts applicants are only half a percentage point more likely to move.
Men and young workers are also more likely to move, the study finds. Men are 3.3 percentage points more likely than women to move. Similarly, a job applicant is seven percentage points less likely to move with each passing decade that they age. Based on the data, employers who want to maintain diverse applicant pools need to also reach candidates that are traditionally less likely to move through more attentive recruiting efforts.
"You might expect that more money would be a top factor for job seekers when considering whether to move for a job, but it's not. Our research shows companies with good culture and employees who love what they do ultimately have a leg-up when it comes to attracting the best talent from across the country," Chamberlain said. "This means employers must ramp-up their recruiting efforts for groups least likely to move – such as women or more senior workers – and have excellent culture, strong pay or benefits offerings."

User: Here is a piece of text: What the neighborhood could and should look like, feel like and include are on the agenda of Thursday's Midtown Ventura Community Council meeting.
What the neighborhood could and should look like, feel like and include in its boundaries is on the agenda of the Midtown Ventura Community Council meeting on Thursday.
The group will be looking at the Ventura Vision, which helped shape the broad plan that guides growth and development in the city. Residents can chime in on what still matters and bring new ideas to help shape the revamp of the 2005 General Plan.
The update to the plan will take place over the next few years. Explore the Ventura Vision at https://bit.ly/2JL908Q.
The city has been looking to update the plan, but the effort was delayed by the Thomas Fire. New City Manager Alex McIntyre is looking at bringing in a consultant to lead the effort and reach out to a broad group of stakeholders.
With the delay, "the time is right to weigh in on the successes we have experienced, and where we would still like to see improvement," the group’s release noted.
Also during the meeting, learn about Bikers Against Child Abuse, a nonprofit that works to give comfort and safety to children who have been victims of abuse. According to the group’s website, "We exist as a body of Bikers to empower children to not feel afraid of the world in which they live."
The group is the first to take part in what will be a regular feature of the meetings to highlight nonprofits and volunteers. Organization representatives will have five minutes to talk about the mission and work and then five minutes to answer questions.
As always, police will also give an update on public safety trends.
Thursday’s meeting will start at 7 p.m. In Cooper Hall, adjacent to Grace Church at MacMillan Ave. For more information, go to midtownventura.org or call chair Dan Long at 805-653-6573.
Keep informed on ways to participate in your backyard. Get a digital subscription to The Star.

The update to the plan will take place over the next few years. Explore the Ventura Vision at https://bit.ly/2JL908Q.
The city has been looking to update the plan, but the effort was delayed by the Thomas Fire. New City Manager Alex McIntyre is looking at bringing in a consultant to lead the effort and reach out to a broad group of stakeholders.
With the delay, "the time is right to weigh in on the successes we have experienced, and where we would still like to see improvement," the group’s release noted.
Also during the meeting, learn about Bikers Against Child Abuse, a nonprofit that works to give comfort and safety to children who have been victims of abuse. According to the group’s website, "We exist as a body of Bikers to empower children to not feel afraid of the world in which they live."
The group is the first to take part in what will be a regular feature of the meetings to highlight nonprofits and volunteers. Organization representatives will have five minutes to talk about the mission and work and then five minutes to answer questions.
As always, police will also give an update on public safety trends.
Thursday’s meeting will start at 7 p.m. In Cooper Hall, adjacent to Grace Church at MacMillan Ave. For more information, go to midtownventura.org or call chair Dan Long at 805-653-6573.
